You express purpose (pour que, afin que, de peur que) and cause with nuance (grâce à, à cause de, faute de, puisque, comme).
I’m writing to you so that you can get organised.
She doesn’t want to leave for fear that her daughter will be cold.
Thanks to your donations, the children will go to Paris.
For lack of time, we won’t visit the Louvre.
Since you’re coming, you can help me.
To express purpose: pour / afin de + infinitive; pour que / afin que + subjunctive.
To express negative purpose: de peur de / de peur que, pour ne pas, pour que… ne… pas.
To tell positive cause (grâce à) from negative cause (à cause de).
To use “faute de” (for lack of) and “à force de” (by dint of).
To tell “puisque” (known cause) from “comme” (at the start of a sentence) and from “parce que”.
Wednesday, 22 January 2030. Julien gathers the parents of the orchestra children to explain how the Paris trip will work. Mrs Mansouri and Mrs Benali, Inès’s mother, have many questions.
Good evening, everyone. I’ve gathered you so that you know exactly how the trip will go. We’ll leave on Saturday 5 April, at seven, by TGV.
Where will the children sleep? I’m afraid they’ll be in a hotel far from the hall.
Thanks to the Philharmonie, we found a youth hostel ten minutes’ walk away. The children will sleep in dormitories of six, girls and boys separately.
And who will watch them at night? Since there will only be twenty adults for sixty children…
There will be one adult in each corridor, all night. We’ve organised shifts so that nobody is too tired on the day of the concert.
I’d like to come as a chaperone. But I work on Saturdays, and since I have no leave left, I don’t know if it’s possible.
As many parents have the same problem, the town hall has written a letter to your employers to explain the situation. I’ll give it to you at the end.
Will Yanis take his cello on the train? I’m afraid someone will break it.
No. For fear that an instrument might get damaged, we’ve hired a small van. The big instruments will travel with Radu, who will leave the day before.
And what if Inès has stage fright? She seems brave, but she hasn’t slept for a week.
That’s normal. With repeated practice, stage fright goes down. And so that they don’t worry too much, we’ll hold a dress rehearsal here, in front of the neighbourhood, on 29 March.
Thank you, Mr Moreau. You’ve reassured us. Well… a little.
A little is already good. I haven’t slept much for a week either.
The golden rule: if the subject is the SAME, use the infinitive; if the subject CHANGES, use “que” + subjunctive.
Je travaille pour payer le voyage.
Je travaille pour que ma fille puisse partir.
Nous répétons afin de jouer mieux.
Je vous écris afin que vous sachiez tout.
“Afin de / afin que” are more formal than “pour / pour que”. You’ll find them in letters and official notices.
A typical mistake: “pour que je puisse” with the same subject ✗ (“Je travaille pour que je puisse partir”). Correct: “Je travaille pour pouvoir partir.”
2. Negative purpose: de peur de / de peur que
He leaves early for fear of missing the train. (same subject)
We hired a van for fear that the instruments might get damaged.
Speak softly so as not to wake the baby.
I close the door so that the cat doesn’t go out.
In formal written French a “ne” with no negative meaning appears: “de peur que les instruments ne soient abîmés”. It is optional and does NOT mean “not”.
3. Cause: grâce à or à cause de?
Grâce à vos dons, les enfants iront à Paris.
À cause de la neige, le train est en retard.
Faute de temps, nous ne visiterons pas le Louvre.
À force de répéter, le trac diminue.
En raison de travaux, la gare est fermée.
Don’t say “grâce à la pluie, le concert est annulé” — it’s ironic! For a negative cause: “à cause de la pluie”.
Je reste parce que je suis malade.
Puisque tu viens, tu peux m’aider.
at the START of the sentence
Comme il pleuvait, nous sommes restés.
Causal “comme” never comes after the main clause. “Nous sommes restés comme il pleuvait” ✗ → “parce qu’il pleuvait”.
Je vous ai réunis afin que…
Nous avons tout prévu pour que…
I’m writing to you so that you know everything.
I work so that I can leave.
He leaves early for fear of missing the train.

With repeated practice, stage fright goes down.
“Because of the snow, the train is late.”
Grâce à la neige, le train est en retard.
Faute de neige, le train est en retard.
Which connector only goes at the start of a sentence?
“I work so that I can leave.”
Je travaille pour que je puisse partir.
Je travaille pour je peux partir.

In January, Julien’s office at the Conservatoire had become a sort of command centre. On the wall he had pinned a big sheet with the names of the sixty children. Next to each name was an empty box. Each time a signed authorisation arrived, he ticked the box in green, with an almost childish pleasure.

In the first weeks the green boxes multiplied very quickly. Thanks to the town hall’s letter, most parents had managed to get a day off. Mrs Benali had even managed to swap her Saturday with a colleague. She would come as a chaperone, to keep an eye on Inès, she said. In reality, everyone knew that above all she wanted to hear her play.

Meanwhile, the rehearsals had changed pace. As the Paris concert would last twenty-five minutes, Julien had chosen four pieces: a Brahms dance, a Spanish folk tune Lucia had taught them, Henri’s waltz and, to finish, the “Waltz for two women” he had composed two years earlier for Hélène and Odile. The children simply called it “Julien’s waltz”.

The Spanish piece was causing problems. The children played too slowly, for fear of making mistakes, and the music lost all its joy. One Wednesday, Lucia came to the rehearsal with her guitar. She clapped her hands, stamped her feet, and made the whole orchestra dance before playing. “Spanish music isn’t played sitting down in your head,” she said. “It’s played with your feet.”

By dint of stamping, the children finally found the rhythm. Yanis laughed so hard he missed three bars. Mrs Roux, sitting on her chair at the back of the hall, beat time with her walking stick, off the beat, but with an enthusiasm that was a pleasure to see. Julien, for his part, wrote in his notebook: “Hire Lucia. For free, if possible.”

On 10 February, there was only one empty box left. It was Sami’s, a little nine-year-old boy who played the flute in the back row. Sami had arrived in La Duchère two years earlier with his father, from a country where there had been a war. He spoke little, but when he played, he closed his eyes and smiled, as if he were somewhere else.

Julien had sent the letter three times. He had phoned, but nobody answered. Sami, for his part, lowered his head whenever anyone mentioned it. “My dad says no,” he finally murmured one Wednesday. “He says Paris is too far.” Then he went back to his seat, his flute clutched to his chest, for fear that it would be taken away too.

That evening Julien told the story at home. Ioana listened while bathing Rose-Hélène, who was splashing everyone and shouting “Paris! Paris!”, the only word she had been repeating for a week. “You can’t force a father,” Ioana said. “But you can try to understand why he’s afraid. If you don’t understand him, you’ll never convince him.”

The next day, Julien talked about it with Mrs Mansouri. She knew Sami’s father. He worked for a cleaning company, at night, like her husband. “He doesn’t read French,” she explained. “He didn’t understand your letter. He only understood the word ‘Paris’ and the word ‘authorisation’. For him, an authorisation is a police paper. He’s afraid of papers.”

Julien was silent. He had never thought of that. He had written his letter carefully, in perfect French, so that it would be clear to everyone. And precisely because of that, it was only clear to those who didn’t need it. “Then we’ll explain it to him differently,” Mrs Mansouri said, putting her headscarf back on. “Tonight. And you’re coming with me.”

Sami’s father lived on the eighth floor of a building where the lift had been broken for three weeks. They climbed on foot, Mrs Mansouri in front, Julien behind, and Odile, who had absolutely insisted on coming, in the middle. She stopped at every floor to catch her breath, but refused any help. “I climbed ship’s ladders for thirty years,” she said. “A block of flats isn’t going to beat me.”

Sami’s father opened the door warily. He was a thin man with grey hair, older than Julien had imagined. The flat was almost empty, but very clean. On the only piece of furniture in the living room was a framed photo: a young woman holding a baby in her arms. Sami had hidden behind the kitchen door.

Mrs Mansouri spoke for a long time, in Arabic, softly. Julien didn’t understand the words, but he understood the tone. She wasn’t trying to convince. She was explaining. From time to time she showed the letter, the drawing of the train Julien had made on a sheet of paper, and the photo of the youth hostel on her phone.

The father listened without saying anything. Then he spoke in turn, and his voice broke in the middle of a sentence. Mrs Mansouri translated, slowly. “He says that the last time he let someone he loved leave, she didn’t come back. He says Sami is all he has left. He says he doesn’t want to be called a bad father, but that he can’t.”

There was a long silence. Nobody looked at the photo on the furniture, but everybody was thinking of it. Julien opened his mouth, then closed it again. There was nothing to say against such a fear. No argument, no “certes… mais”, no official letter could make it disappear.

It was Odile who spoke first. She leaned towards Sami’s father and put her wrinkled hand on his. “Sir,” she said, very slowly, so that Mrs Mansouri would have time to translate. “I too waited for a sailor for months, on every voyage. I know what it’s like. So I’m going to make you a proposal.”

“Since you’re afraid to let your son go, come with him. You’ll be a chaperone. You can sleep in the corridor, in front of his door, if you like. And as you work nights, you’ll be the best night watchman we have.” The father looked at Odile, then at Mrs Mansouri, then at Julien. “And my job?” he asked, in French this time.

Julien had at last found something useful to say. “I’ll call your boss tomorrow morning. The town hall has written a letter to all employers. And if that’s not enough, I know a city councillor who owes me a favour.” He was thinking of Bernard Delorme. He was sure that Delorme, after his ten scarves, couldn’t refuse.

Sami’s father thought for a long time again. Then he called his son. Sami came out of the kitchen shyly, flute in hand. His father said something to him in Arabic, very quietly. The boy’s face was transformed all at once, like when you switch on the light in a dark room. He ran to his room and came back with a pen.

The father signed the authorisation slowly, pressing hard, like someone who doesn’t often get the chance to write his name. Then he signed a second sheet, the one for chaperones. Odile clapped. Mrs Mansouri took out of her bag, as if by magic, a box of cakes she had brought “just in case”.

On the stairs, on the way down, Julien asked Odile: “And you, are you coming to Paris?” She stopped on a step. “Dr Martin says I can, provided I take the lift and don’t carry anything. I’ll sleep at Isabelle’s. I haven’t been to Paris since her wedding, in 1998. Henri wore the navy suit. The one you wore on your wedding day.”

That same day, Julien called the boss of Sami’s father. The man refused at first: he was short-staffed, Saturday was a busy day, he couldn’t make exceptions. Julien then called Bernard Delorme. An hour later, the boss called back. He had changed his mind. He even offered to pay for the day off, “so that the company can also take part in this fine project”.

Julien never found out what Delorme had said on the phone. When he wanted to thank him, the councillor simply replied: “I didn’t do anything. I only reminded the gentleman that he had a contract with the city. And that contracts with the city are renewed every year.” Then he added, with a little laugh: “Admittedly, it’s not very elegant. But it works.”

The next morning, Julien coloured the last box green. He stood for a while in front of the wall, looking at the sixty green boxes. Then he took a photo and sent it to Ioana, without comment. She replied with a single word: “Bravo.” And, two minutes later, with a second photo: Rose-Hélène, in pyjamas, holding a plastic flute upside down.

Marc Delorme wanted to write an article about Sami. Julien refused. “Some stories aren’t meant for newspapers,” he explained. “They belong to the people who live them.” Marc thought about it, then nodded. Instead he wrote an article about the chaperones: twenty adults, twenty jobs, twenty reasons to go to Paris. Sami’s father appeared in it, without a name, as “a night watchman who will not sleep”.

Ioana, for her part, had another worry. Rose-Hélène’s birthday fell on 4 March, a month before Paris, and she wanted to organise a small party. But Julien came home late every evening, his notebook full of lists, and Radu spent his weekends preparing the wedding. “Since nobody has time,” she decided, “it’ll be a simple party. A cake, candles and the family.” She already knew it wouldn’t be simple at all.

Meanwhile, at the other end of Europe, another operation was being set up. In Iași, Ioana and Radu’s grandmother had announced that she would come to her grandson’s wedding in May. By coach, of course. Costel, the driver, had already promised to keep her the same seat as in 2027, right behind him, “so that she can keep an eye on the road”.

Elena and Dan, on the other hand, would fly, because of work. Elena had already prepared a list of forty-three things not to forget. Dan had started brushing up his French with an old textbook from the eighties, and he said to everyone “Comment allez-vous, mon cher ?” with an accent that made Radu laugh on the phone.

In Seville, doña Carmen was sewing Lucia’s dress in secret, in the back bedroom. Nobody was allowed in, not even don Manuel, for fear that he would describe it to someone. Don Manuel, for his part, was rehearsing every evening a song he had composed for the bride and groom. He hadn’t told anyone about it, except his guitar.

Radu and Lucia, meanwhile, had spent a whole Sunday choosing the wedding music. Lucia wanted flamenco, Radu wanted a hora, and they both wanted Henri’s waltz. “As we can’t have everything,” Radu suggested, “we could do a programme in three parts.” Lucia looked at him tenderly. “My love, at a Spanish and Romanian wedding you can have everything. You just have to dance until six in the morning.”

Radu did the maths and turned pale. Then he thought of his grandmother, who had danced the hora until two in the morning at Ioana’s wedding, at over eighty. And of don Manuel, who, according to Lucia, had never left a party before sunrise. He understood he would not win this battle. So he decided not to start it.

The following Wednesday, at rehearsal, Sami arrived first, even before Yanis. His father came with him. He sat at the back of the hall, on Mrs Roux’s chair, and listened to the whole rehearsal without moving. At the end, he came to shake Julien’s hand. He said only one word, in French, searching for it for a long time: “Thank you.” Then, after a moment: “Paris.” And for the first time since Julien had known him, Sami laughed out loud, a real happy child’s laugh, clear and ringing, that echoed all the way up to the ceiling window.

Reading text: The letter to the parents
The Conservatoire sends an official letter to the families. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Dear Sir or Madam, we are pleased to confirm that your child will take part in the concert of the “Musique en partage” orchestra at the Philharmonie de Paris on Sunday 6 April 2030.
Thanks to the generosity of the residents of La Duchère and of several donors, the trip will be entirely free for families. We thank them warmly.
So that the stay goes as smoothly as possible, we ask you to fill in the enclosed trip authorisation and return it to us before 15 February.
Without a signed authorisation, we will unfortunately not be able to take your child. As the number of seats on the train is limited, no exceptions will be possible.
Each child must bring a sleeping bag, warm clothes and a black outfit for the concert. So that nothing gets lost, please write the child’s name on all their belongings.
For any question, do not hesitate to contact Mr Julien Moreau. Yours faithfully, Claire Vasseur, Director of the Conservatoire.
Combien coûte le voyage pour les familles ?
Avant quelle date faut-il retourner l’autorisation ?
Que faut-il écrire sur les affaires ?
